title: Colic in Babies: Signs, Soothing and When to Get Help
description: Is it colic? The signs of colic in babies, soothing techniques that may help, how to cope with a crying baby and when crying means you should call a doctor.
intro: Hours of crying you can’t seem to settle is exhausting and upsetting. Colic is common, it doesn’t last forever, and you are not doing anything wrong.

image.alt: A man carrying and comforting a baby

sections.html: Colic is when a healthy baby cries a lot without an obvious reason. The NHS says it is common in the first few weeks and usually stops by around 3 to 4 months (sometimes 6 months). Crying in all babies tends to peak at around 6 to 8 weeks.

• Intense crying for more than 3 hours a day, 3 days a week, for at least a week
  • Crying that's often in the late afternoon or evening
  • Hard to soothe or settle
  • Clenched fists, a red face, arching the back, or bringing the knees up to the tummy

Hold and move

Hold your baby close, rock, sway or walk with them, or use a sling.

White noise

Gentle shushing, a fan or calm background sound.

Warm bath

Some babies relax in a warm (not hot) bath.

Feeding checks

Wind during and after feeds; ask about bottle position or latch.

Fresh air

A walk in the pram or carrier.

Swap with someone

Tag-team with a partner, family or friend.

The NHS says there is little evidence for most colic remedies sold in shops, so speak to a pharmacist or health visitor before buying anything. Don't change your baby's formula without advice.

sections.h2: Coping when the crying won’t stop
sections.html: It is completely normal to feel frustrated. If you feel overwhelmed, put your baby down safely on their back in their cot, close the door, and take a few minutes to calm down. Never shake a baby; it can cause serious brain injury. The UK's ICON programme has practical tips. Cry-sis (UK) offers a helpline for parents of crying babies.

Get medical advice if your baby's cry sounds different (high-pitched or weak), they have a temperature of 38°C or higher (under 3 months), they're not feeding or have fewer wet nappies, they vomit green, have blood in their poo, or seem floppy or unwell. Call 999 / 911 if they have trouble breathing or are unresponsive.

faqs.a: Colic usually improves by 3 to 4 months, and almost always by 6 months, according to the NHS.

faqs.q: Can breastfeeding mums change their diet to help colic?
faqs.a: Sometimes a health professional may suggest cutting out certain foods if there’s a sign of allergy, but don’t make big changes without advice. Talk to your GP, health visitor or paediatrician.
